Water first. Substrate second. 💧🌱 This is personally my favorite way to add substrate, especially for a no CO₂, no-filter aquarium. I start with about 2 cm of water, then add the substrate directly into it. The water immediately traps most of the fine particles, instead of letting a cloud of dust spread everywhere. I also don’t rinse my substrate, because I prefer to keep everything it contains rather than washing part of the fine material away. Less dust. Less mess. Nothing wasted. An aquarium’s filter does far more than keep the water looking clean. It continuously removes waste, circulates oxygen, and provides a home for beneficial bacteria that break down harmful toxins produced by fish and uneaten food. Without proper filtration, ammonia and other toxic compounds can quickly build up, turning a healthy aquarium into a dangerous environment for its inhabitants. A good filtration system helps maintain water quality, stabilize the ecosystem, and keep fish healthy over the long term. While decorations and lighting may catch the eye, the filter is the unseen engine that keeps the entire aquarium alive.

Cleaning a fish tank doesn't always mean draining it. In this method, waste and debris are removed while the water stays in place. Tools like siphon vacuums and filtration systems pull out uneaten food, algae, and sediment from the gravel, keeping the environment clean without stressing the fish. What makes this approach effective is balance. Beneficial bacteria remain undisturbed, water chemistry stays stable, and the tank continues to cycle naturally. It's a low-impact way to maintain a healthy aquarium, showing how smart maintenance can work with the ecosystem instead of resetting it. This video is for educational purposes only. The amount of times I hear “Your tank looks dirty, why don’t you clean it” is ridiculous (I am looking at you @Fish Shop Matt).  Water that is tinted a yellowy brown doesn’t always mean the tank is overdue a water change. Instead, many fishkeepers (like me!) do this on purpose to recreate the natural habitats of our fishes more closely.  The tinted water helps to create the dim and gloomy conditions of forest streams and swamps. Plus, the weakly acidic tannic and humic substances help to lower the pH, which is beneficial for many of the fishes we keep in aquariums. Next time you see a “tinted” aquarium I urge you to look a little closer, you may find beauty hidden in those gloomy waters. 🍂
